text.p: Sasha Danilovic, the Miami Heat's smooth-shooting guard from Serbia, was a perfect 7-for-7 from 3-point range in a convincing win over the New York Knicks Tuesday, but afterwards downplayed his personal heroics.

"Really it wasn't a big deal," Danilovic, a member of Yugoslavia's silver-medal Olympic team this summer, said after the first-place Heat's 99-75 victory over a key Atlantic Division rival. "I feel very happy, first of all, because we won, and then, because I shot well."

Danilovic, whose rookie NBA campaign last season was a washout because of injury, refused to say he felt especially good about his 21 points, second high in the game to teammate Dan Majerle's 22: "Not any better than the other wins that we've had, believe me."
The 26-year-old guard, the team's fourth-leading scorer this season, shot 7-for-8 with two rebounds, one assist and two steals. He also turned the ball over a game-high six times, however.
Coach Pat Riley spread the credit around for the win, saying initially of the 6-foot-6 (1.98 m) Serb only that "I think Danilovic is starting to feel very comfortable with the game."
Riley did not feel it was Danilovic's best NBA game. "He's had a couple really good games. But he really shot the ball well," said Riley.
Danilovic's teammates repeatedly found him standing alone on the 3-point arc.
"Guys were looking at me. I was wide open. They got me the ball at the right time and I was making those shots, that's it -- nothing special. I could have missed them. I didn't."
Danilovic acknowledged there was a special rivalry between Riley and the Knicks team he left under acrimonious circumstances a little over a season ago.
"This was a particular game, probably, not so much for me but for coach and some of the players," Danilovic said.

Danilovic finally conceded that having such a hot shooting touch had felt a little special. "If I make seven 3's against little kids I would be happy," he said, provoking a heckling cry of "What?" from Majerle sitting next to him in the crowded visitors' locker room at Madison Square Garden.
The two began to jokingly insult each other, the young Serb a little more clumsily than the veteran Majerle, who offered to "translate" Danilovic's perfectly adequate English.

Savoring the moment of camaraderie but suddenly remembering the gruelling NBA marathon still ahead of him, Danilovic, looking tired but laughing almost giddily, explained to reporters: "We just enjoy these 15, 20 minutes, and then tomorrow it's another game."
